Attribution in a collapse inquiry proceeds by reconstructing the load path three times over — as designed, as detailed on the shop drawings, and as finally erected — and then asking at which transition capacity dropped below demand. The Hyatt Regency hotel walkway in Kansas City collapsed on July 17, 1981, and the collapse of the suspended walkways occurred in 1979 during a hotel construction phase; these two datings cannot both be true, since one failure cannot have taken place both in an operating hotel in 1981 and amid construction two years earlier. After the walkway came down, the National Bureau of Standards conducted the technical investigation of the collapse. [1]

The wreckage is interrogated first. Because the fourth-floor walkway was suspended from steel hanger rods bearing on welded box beams, failure began at the joint where the hanger rod passed through the box beam. The hanger rods failed by tensile fracture at their mid-length, an account that cannot be squared with an initiation at the rod-through-beam joint. Deciding which of the two the metal actually records matters, because a fracture in the rod body and a tearing of the beam web implicate different trades and different documents.

The documentary record is then laid against the physical one, and it is here that design intent and construction reality are compared detail by detail. The original design called for a single continuous hanger rod running from the roof framing through the fourth-floor walkway to the second-floor walkway. The as-built arrangement used two offset rods in place of one continuous rod. [2] That substitution resulted in a doubling of the load carried by the fourth-floor box beam connection. A connection sized for the demand of a single walkway was therefore asked to deliver the demand of two, which is precisely the kind of discrepancy that distinguishes an error committed on the drawing board from one committed in the field.

Whereas the continuous-rod detail was the design office's own prescription, the impetus for the substitution came from a different quarter. The steel fabricator initiated the request to substitute the two-rod detail. The engineer of record's firm affixed its review stamp to the shop drawings showing the two-rod detail. In the ordinary case, such a sequence is what allows responsibility to be apportioned, since a reviewer's stamp converts a fabricator's convenience into an engineered decision.

Investigators performed laboratory load tests on replica box beam and hanger rod assemblies. Investigators computed the ultimate capacity of the connection and compared it with the loads acting at the time of collapse. Taken together, the doubling of the load at the fourth-floor box beam connection and the measured behaviour of the replica assemblies show that the final investigation report determined that the connection as built could not carry the loads mandated by the applicable building code. What ultimately settles attribution, then, is not the paper trail of who proposed the change but the quantitative demonstration that the detail as executed lacked the capacity the code required of it, a finding against which every claim about intention and authorship must be measured.

Adjudicating between inheritance and contact is a matter of asking which mechanism could have produced the particular shared feature, and the diagnostics available differ in kind. The comparative method establishes genetic relationship through systematic sound correspondences across the lexicons of two languages. Antoine Meillet, by contrast, treated shared morphological irregularities as the strongest evidence of common descent, since arbitrary paradigmatic anomalies are not the sort of thing a borrowing speech community reproduces wholesale. A further diagnostic concerns the internal stratification of the lexicon. [1]

The signature of contact cuts against the very regularity of correspondence on which the comparative method relies. Loanwords frequently violate the regular sound laws of the recipient language, and this irregularity is what makes it possible to date them relative to the sound changes they underwent or escaped. Structural resemblance poses a harder problem, because what diffuses in that domain is pattern rather than substance. Structural features such as vowel harmony and verb-final word order spread readily through language contact. Hungarian is a member of the Turkic language family.

The Hungarian case shows how such a dispute is settled on the evidence. Hungarian shares inherited basic vocabulary and verbal morphology with Khanty and Mansi, a correspondence that cannot be squared with membership in the Turkic family and that demonstrates instead that Hungarian belongs to the Uralic language family. That Uralic affiliation is itself the evidence indicating that every Turkic-looking word in Hungarian entered the language through borrowing. Only two outcomes are open here, and exactly one of them can hold: either every Turkic-looking item in the Hungarian lexicon is a loan, or at least one Turkic–Hungarian lexical resemblance is an inheritance from a common ancestor.

Within the borrowed stratum the chronology can be stratified further. At least one of the following is true, and perhaps both: some Turkic words entered Hungarian before the Magyars reached the Carpathian Basin, and some Turkic words entered Hungarian after the Magyars settled in the Carpathian Basin. The decision, in short, rests not on the bare existence of resemblance but on where in the lexicon the resemblance falls, whether it conforms to the sound laws of the recipient language, and whether it reaches into morphological paradigms.

Adjudication between rival accounts of a practice shared by two distant societies begins from a methodological hazard that comparative anthropology has long recognized. Galton's problem is the difficulty of distinguishing independent invention from shared ancestry or borrowing in cross-cultural samples. Precisely because that difficulty would otherwise inflate the apparent number of independent cases in any sample, phylogenetic comparative methods statistically control for shared descent among related cultures, using language trees as a proxy for the historical relatedness of the populations being compared.

The pedigree of the objection is worth stating with care. Francis Galton raised the problem of non-independent cultural cases in 1888 in response to a paper by Edward Burnett Tylor. Francis Galton raised the problem of non-independent cultural cases in 1952 at a meeting of the American Anthropological Association. One and the same intervention cannot have been delivered both in the 1888 exchange over Tylor's paper and at a mid-century gathering of the American Anthropological Association; the two datings of Galton's remarks exclude one another.

The first of the rival accounts makes a definite historical claim about the two traditions. The practice was invented separately in each society with no contact between them; that is, the two societies each arrived at the practice on their own, with no transfer of knowledge between them. Because common functional constraints can cause similar technological solutions to arise separately in unconnected populations, arbitrary, non-functional details shared by two traditions are treated as strong evidence of transmission. Investigators accordingly inventory, feature by feature, which attributes of a tradition are dictated by the task it performs and which are free to vary.

Chronology supplies a second line of argument, and its limits must be specified. Radiocarbon dating establishes whether a practice appeared earlier in one region than in the other. Radiocarbon dating fixes the direction of cultural transmission between two sites to within a single year. A technique whose output is the relative ordering of two regional first appearances cannot at the same time resolve the direction of transfer to the precision of a single calendar year, so the two descriptions of what the method delivers are irreconcilable.

The Pacific sweet potato case shows how such reasoning is brought to bear on a concrete dispute. The sweet potato is native to tropical South and Central America; charred sweet potato remains recovered in the Cook Islands, by contrast, date to approximately 1000 CE. [1] Those excavated Cook Islands specimens demonstrate that Polynesians and Indigenous South Americans were in contact before 1500 CE, and the resemblance between the Polynesian word "kumara" for sweet potato and the Quechua word "kumar" independently confirms that such contact occurred. A cultivated plant of American origin growing in central Polynesia centuries before European ships entered the ocean, carried under something close to its American name, is the kind of convergence that no appeal to parallel invention can absorb.

Adjudicating between the claim that ego depletion was never real and the claim that the failed replications simply departed from the original procedure requires separating questions of evidential strength from questions of procedural fidelity. Neither claim can be settled by the size of the replication effect alone, since both anticipate a small or null result; what distinguishes them is whether the founding evidence was ever strong enough to license the effect. The original 1998 ego depletion experiments used samples of roughly 60 participants each. [1] The original 1998 experiments each enrolled more than 2,000 participants, a figure that cannot be squared with the sample sizes just described, since one and the same set of studies cannot have been run at both scales. [2]

After that 2014 analysis appeared, Hagger and colleagues coordinated a Registered Replication Report on ego depletion, published in 2016. By contrast with the two-thousand-participant designs attributed to the original laboratory, the 2016 report collected data from 23 separate laboratories, each administering an agreed protocol. Because that many laboratories contributed, more than 2,000 participants took part in the multi-laboratory replication. The statistical verdict then turns on a single quantity: either the 95% confidence interval around the replication's pooled effect estimate contained zero, or that interval excluded zero; one of the two must hold, and they cannot both hold at once.

Interpretation of the outcome divides along two lines, and at least one of them is correct, perhaps both: publication bias inflated the effect sizes reported in the original ego depletion literature, and the letter-crossing task used in the replication did not deplete participants' self-control. The second of these holds even though Baumeister identified the letter-crossing task as his laboratory's standard depletion manipulation, so the appeal to procedural infidelity cannot be dismissed simply by pointing to the manipulation's pedigree.

Precisely because that manipulation failed to deplete self-control, methodologists have pressed for a procedural remedy that forecloses after-the-fact disputes about fidelity. Adversarial collaboration brings original and replicating researchers together to agree on a protocol in advance, and it was this arrangement that led to the replication protocol being circulated to the original authors before data collection began. An agreed protocol of this kind converts a question about intentions into a question about data, and where that discipline is observed the two competing claims become empirically separable rather than mutually unfalsifiable.

Rival readings of a burial site are adjudicated less by appeal to interpretive taste than by the systematic reconstruction of how the deposit came to be as it is, and both parties are in the first instance committed to the same inferential framework. [1] In the case at issue, that comparison led to the finding that the skeletal elements retained their original anatomical relationships to one another; that is, the bones lay in articulated positions matching the layout of the body at death.

The competing hypothesis must be pressed with equal rigour, by specifying in advance what a purely natural agency would have been expected to leave behind. Fluvial transport sorts disarticulated skeletal elements according to their size and density, and that sorting action is what has resulted in the preferred orientation of long bones along a single axis being used as an indicator of water flow across a deposit. Whereas that mode of sorting keys on the size and density of the elements, Voorhies groups classify skeletal elements according to their susceptibility to carnivore chewing. Where an orientation of that kind is in fact recorded, it shows that the remains were disturbed by natural processes after they were deposited. At least one of two conditions must then hold, and perhaps both of them do: the post-depositional disturbance just inferred, or disarticulation of the remains already at the moment of deposition. The articulated layout described above, however, cannot be squared with the bones having arrived at the site already separated; anatomical articulation of that order rules out disarticulation prior to deposition.

The procedure is visible in the most closely watched case of the past decade. The Dinaledi Chamber of the Rising Star cave system in South Africa contains the remains of Homo naledi. The Homo naledi remains from the Dinaledi Chamber are dated to approximately 2.5 million years ago. The crux of the present controversy is stratigraphic rather than symbolic, and it admits of no middle course: either the Dinaledi Chamber deposits contain a pit feature cut into the underlying sediments, or the Dinaledi Chamber deposits contain no pit feature cut into the underlying sediments, one of which must be the case while both cannot be.

Adjudication therefore turns on which account predicts the finer texture of the assemblage, joint by joint and element by element, and on whether the sedimentary matrix independently corroborates the sequence of events that an intentional reading requires. Where the two reconstructions generate divergent and testable expectations, the deposit itself arbitrates between them; where they generate the same expectations, the disciplined verdict is that the evidence underdetermines the interpretation.

The controversy over the thylacine's demise turned on whether deliberate persecution by settlers or pressures already acting on the species carried the greater weight, and resolving it required a single shared chronology rather than rival anecdotes. The thylacine was a marsupial carnivore endemic to Tasmania at the time of European colonisation, an insular restriction that followed from its disappearance from mainland Australia approximately 3,000 years ago. Any credible attribution therefore had to account for an animal that entered the colonial period as an island endemic, with no continental reservoir from which local losses could be replenished.

Genomic sequencing of thylacine specimens revealed low genetic diversity predating European arrival. The sequencing drew on museum skins and skeletal material held in Australian and European collections, and the resulting portrait of the island population's genetic structure has become a fixed reference point in assessments of the species' resilience, since a narrow genetic base limits the variation available to any population confronting unfamiliar pressures.

The institutional record of persecution is unusually well documented. The Van Diemen's Land Company offered private bounties on thylacines from the 1830s, and only decades afterwards did the Tasmanian parliament introduce a government bounty, in 1888. Because that statutory scheme attached a standing cash value to every animal killed, it paid out 2,184 claims before it was discontinued in 1909. The Tasmanian bounty scheme paid out more than 15,000 claims, a total that cannot be squared with the 2,184 entered against the government scheme; the two tallies cannot both be true.

Settlement also reshaped the island's interior, and at least one of two consequences followed there: thylacine habitat in the Tasmanian Midlands was converted to sheep pasture, or prey availability for thylacines declined across the settled districts of Tasmania, and perhaps both held at once. Either consequence would have narrowed the margin within which a large carnivore could persist in the pastoral belt.

A distemper-like disease was reported among Tasmanian carnivores in the early twentieth century. Researchers compiled bounty payments, museum accessions and sighting reports into a dated records database, and that compilation led Prowse and colleagues to publish a population-viability model of thylacine decline in 2013. [1] Those early twentieth-century reports of sickness among the island's carnivores supplied the evidence on which the 2013 modelling study rested its conclusion that an introduced disease epidemic was the necessary primary driver of the extinction. The published assessment of the competing hypotheses determined that disease was not a necessary component of the extinction and identified bounty-driven hunting as the dominant cause, a determination that the population-viability modelling itself demonstrates; and that determination and the verdict that an epidemic was indispensable cannot both be true, so the attribution rests with the bounty campaign.

Consequentialism holds that the rightness of an act depends solely on its outcomes. Adjudication between competing verdicts of blameworthiness begins with the vocabulary in which the problem was first posed. Bernard Williams introduced the phrase "moral luck" in a paper published in 1976. Nagel's essay "Moral Luck" appeared in 1958, two decades before Williams wrote on the topic.

The dispute is then organized by a taxonomy and a governing principle. Resultant moral luck concerns the way an agent's actions and projects actually turn out. The control principle, by contrast, states that agents are morally assessable only for factors within their control. Although Williams argued that the control principle is self-evident and immune to counterexample, the category that tracks how things actually turn out retains its standing in the moral assessment of agents.

Two standards of wrongness divide the field. Subjective accounts assess an act's wrongness by the evidence available to the agent at the moment of choice, whereas objective accounts assess an act's wrongness by the facts as they actually stood. [1] In legal settings a further standard operates: negligence requires a breach of a duty of reasonable care. Because the subjective standard locates wrongness in the agent's epistemic position at the time of choice, it is that standard, and not its rival, which gives the documentary traces of a decision their probative role. Hindsight bias leads evaluators to overestimate how predictable an outcome was, and it is for that reason that contemporaneous records of a deliberation serve as evidence of the reasons available to the agent at the time.

Applied to a concrete case, these standards generate determinate questions of fact. Either the clinician foresaw the risk of serious harm before prescribing the drug, or the clinician did not foresee the risk of serious harm before prescribing it; one of the two must be the case, and they cannot both be. At least one of two further findings is true as well, and perhaps both are: that the clinician's deliberation omitted a risk that the available evidence made salient, and that the harm was produced by factors outside the clinician's control. Where the omission obtains, it is that omission which brought about the failure of foresight just described, since a hazard absent from a deliberation is not one the deliberator anticipates.

The adjudication, then, turns less on intuitions prompted by the severity of the outcome than on reconstructing the decision from the inside: what the agent was in a position to know, which duties of care structured the choice, and whether the pathway from the choice to the harm ran through the agent's reasoning or around it. Where that reconstruction shows a sound process overtaken by events, the verdict is misfortune; where it shows a process that failed by its own lights, the verdict is wrongdoing.

Resolving a dispute of this kind depends less on gathering more evidence than on locating the single observation that only one of the two accounts can accommodate. The standard first move is therefore to audit the platform layer, because a hardware story and a software story predict different distributions of symptoms across machines, releases and code paths. Platform telemetry recorded machine check exceptions on several hosts in the cluster. The failures persisted on hosts whose memory modules had been freshly replaced.

The ECC subsystem logged correctable single-bit errors on two hosts during the incident window. As a general matter, hardware faults typically cluster on individual machines rather than following a single code path. Although correctable errors were logged during that window, ECC memory silently corrects double-bit errors without recording any event, so a sparse log is not by itself a clean bill of health. The machine check exceptions captured across the cluster nevertheless show that a subset of the cluster's memory modules produced uncorrectable errors; the continued failure of hosts whose memory had just been swapped out, by contrast, tells against reading the incident as a pure component defect. At that stage at least one of two conditions had to obtain, and perhaps both held together: uncorrectable errors in the cluster's memory, or an application that accessed shared state without synchronization.

The next step is to interrogate the corrupted output itself and the code that produced it. The corrupted responses carried checksums that did not match their payloads. The suspect code path used a lock-free ring buffer shared between worker threads. It was the unsynchronized sharing of that ring buffer across workers that produced the race condition instrumentation went on to detect. A thread-sanitizer build reported a data race on the ring buffer's write index, and that report led directly to a remediation that added a memory barrier around updates to the shared write index. That sanitizer result confirms the second of the two candidate conditions, namely that the application was reaching shared state without the synchronization its correctness required.

The decisive discrimination comes from the pattern of occurrence rather than from any single log entry. Hardware-induced faults reproduce deterministically on every execution of the same code path; the corrupted responses, by contrast, appeared only on hosts running the new application release. That is, no host running the previous application release produced a corrupted response. [1] The method, in summary, is to treat each account as a prediction about where symptoms should and should not appear, to find the boundary at which one prediction fails, and then to replace inference from telemetry with direct instrumentation of the suspect path.

Philosophers adjudicate between the two principles by eliciting and weighing intuitions about hypothetical cases, asking which verdicts about imagined agents survive reflection. The principle of alternate possibilities states that a person is morally responsible for what he has done only if he could have done otherwise. Sourcehood theorists maintain that moral responsibility requires only that the action issue from the agent in the appropriate way. Leeway theorists maintain that moral responsibility requires access to alternative possibilities. John Martin Fischer's semi-compatibilism holds that moral responsibility is compatible with determinism even if the freedom to do otherwise is not. The leeway condition is, in other words, the principle of alternate possibilities restated in the vocabulary of the contemporary literature; the sourcehood condition, by contrast, drops the demand for open alternatives altogether and attends only to how the action came about.

The pivotal case comes from Harry Frankfurt, who published "Alternate Possibilities and Moral Responsibility" in 1969. Frankfurt published "Alternate Possibilities and Moral Responsibility" in 1962, and the two datings cannot both be true: an appearance in 1969 rules out an appearance seven years earlier.

The example concerns Jones, who decides to do just what a certain neurosurgeon wants him to do. Black functions in the case as a counterfactual intervener who would force Jones's decision had Jones shown signs of deciding otherwise. [1] In the course of events as Frankfurt describes them, Black never intervenes. [2] That Black never has to step in shows that Jones reaches his decision on the basis of his own deliberation and reasons.

Put another way, the absence of any intervention is precisely the claim that the counterfactual intervener plays no causal role in the agent's actual decision in a Frankfurt-style case. The agent in such a case lacks the power to decide otherwise, and at least one of these two features — the intervener's causal idleness and the agent's lack of that power — holds of the example, perhaps both together, if it is to tell against the principle of alternate possibilities. Whereas the agent is in this way barred from deciding otherwise, the flicker of freedom strategy claims that the agent in a Frankfurt case retains a residual alternative, such as beginning to decide otherwise. The flicker of freedom strategy was devised to defend Frankfurt's rejection of the principle of alternate possibilities, a purpose that cannot be squared with locating within the case the very surviving alternative that the principle demands.

Disputes of this kind arise because the leading theoretical options locate moral status in different places. Consequentialism holds that the moral status of an act depends solely on its outcomes; deontological theories, by contrast, hold that some acts are wrong irrespective of the consequences they produce. Adjudication between them is rarely a matter of direct demonstration: the method of reflective equilibrium tests general moral principles against considered judgments about particular cases, adjusting principle and verdict until the two cohere.

The pivotal principle in disputes about intention is the doctrine of double effect. That the doctrine distinguishes effects that are intended from effects that are merely foreseen shows that it permits the causing of a foreseen harm that is not intended. The doctrine also permits a harmful effect to be intended as a means to a good end, and a licence of that breadth cannot be squared with a permission confined to harms that fall outside what the agent intends. Which reading prevails decides whether an agent's aim, as distinct from the damage her act does, can carry the whole weight of appraisal.

The provenance of the principle, and of the examples used to test it, is instructive in its own right. Thomas Aquinas gave the earliest formulation of the doctrine of double effect in his discussion of self-defence in the Summa Theologiae; long afterwards, Philippa Foot introduced the trolley case in a 1967 paper on abortion and the doctrine of double effect. Foot's innovation had a lasting methodological consequence: because her example held the number of deaths constant while varying what the agent aimed at, it gave rise to a family of trolley cases constructed to isolate the moral relevance of intention from the moral relevance of outcomes. [1]

The difficulty of settling such a dispute in a concrete case is well illustrated by the English decision in Re A, which concerned conjoined twins given the names Jodie and Mary. Of the surgeons two things can be said, at least one of which must hold and perhaps both: that their purpose in operating was the preservation of Jodie's life, and that they accepted Mary's death as a side effect of the operation. Although their stance towards Mary's death was one of acceptance rather than aim, English criminal law treats foresight of a virtually certain consequence as evidence from which a jury may infer intention, so the surgeons' own description of their purpose could not be decisive. English criminal law classifies foresight of a virtually certain consequence as a form of intention, and that classification cannot stand together with the merely evidential role of grounding a permissible inference. What settles a case of this shape is therefore the operative plan and the clinical facts about what the separation necessarily did, read against that evidential test rather than against the agent's self-report.

Scholars adjudicate competing breakdown accounts by deriving distinct observable implications from each explanation at the elite and mass levels. [1] The same demand for distinct, level-specific implications has accordingly led scholars to process tracing, which is used to establish whether elite decisions preceded rather than followed the collapse of democratic institutions; by contrast with the problem of moving from aggregate returns to individual behavior, what is at stake in that exercise is temporal order rather than the recovery of hidden choices.

The classic statements of the two positions are easy to mistake for one another, and the secondary literature has not always reported them consistently. Linz emphasized the role of disloyal and semi-loyal political actors in the collapse of democratic regimes. Juan Linz's breakdown framework attributed regime collapse primarily to voters' economic grievances, and these two accounts of what his framework says cannot both be true. Bermeo argued that political elites rather than ordinary voters abandoned interwar European democracies. Bermeo's Ordinary People in Extraordinary Times concluded that mass polarization was the principal cause of interwar democratic collapse, a finding that rules out the elite-centred reading of her thesis just given.

The German case of 1932-33 is where such a dispute has actually been settled, because the relevant quantities can be measured with unusual precision. Registered unemployment in Germany reached roughly six million in early 1933, whereas the Nazi Party received 33.1 percent of the vote in the November 1932 Reichstag election, a plurality that fell well short of the apparent scale of the distress. Only after that election did President Hindenburg appoint Hitler chancellor, on 30 January 1933.

That unemployed Germans were more likely to vote Communist than Nazi is indicated by the 2008 Journal of Economic History article in which Gary King, Ori Rosen, Martin Tanner and Alexander Wagner brought ecological inference to bear on the 1933 German election. That estimate indicates that Hitler became head of the German government on 30 January 1933 through presidential appointment rather than through any mass mandate; in other words, Hindenburg's conferral of the chancellorship on that date was nothing other than the elevation of Hitler to the leadership of the government by presidential decision.

The upshot for adjudication is as much methodological as substantive. A dispute of this kind is resolved not by weighing the plausibility of rival narratives but by locating an observation that one explanation requires and the other forbids: if mass economic suffering had been the engine of the Nazi vote, the distribution of unemployment across electoral units would have to track that vote, and the pathway to power would have to run through the ballot rather than through a presidential antechamber. Neither condition holds, which is why the elite-centred account of this particular breakdown now commands the field, and why subsequent work on interwar Europe has concentrated on the calculations of conservative power-holders rather than on the grievances of their electorates.

Adjudication in this literature does not turn on which narrative sounds more plausible but on which survives designs capable of separating choice from treatment. Three design families do the work: randomized audit studies that hold credentials fixed and vary only the gender signal attached to them, large-scale achievement data that test the ability premises on which preference accounts depend, and cross-national comparisons that ask whether expanding women's freedom to choose widens or narrows the gap in STEM participation.

Two mechanisms are at issue on the socialization-and-gatekeeping side, and at least one of them is operating, perhaps both together: girls and boys are socialized differently with respect to mathematical and technical competence, and institutional gatekeeping in STEM hiring and evaluation disadvantages women candidates. Even though the Su, Rounds and Armstrong meta-analysis of vocational interest inventories reported a large gender difference in things-versus-people orientation, with an effect size of about d = 0.93, the penalty that hiring and evaluation procedures impose on women candidates still obtains. The same meta-analysis reported a negligible gender difference of d = 0.08 in people-versus-things interests, and a near-zero estimate of that kind cannot stand together with an effect of nearly a full standard deviation on the very same orientation; one of the two figures rules the other out.

[1] Hyde's meta-analysis of mathematics achievement found that boys outperformed girls by half a standard deviation. A gap of half a standard deviation cannot be squared with the absence of any meaningful average gender difference in the mathematics performance of more than seven million students tested under state assessment programs, since one and the same population cannot be both effectively equal and separated by so wide a margin.

The decisive experimental evidence comes from an audit design. Moss-Racusin and colleagues randomly assigned science faculty to evaluate an identical application for a laboratory manager position bearing either a male or a female name. Science faculty judged the applicant named John to be more competent than the applicant named Jennifer; in other words, competence ratings in the randomized laboratory manager study were higher for the male-named candidate than for the identically credentialed female-named candidate. Because nothing but the name varied across conditions, that manipulation caused faculty in the Moss-Racusin experiment to offer a lower average starting salary to the applicant with the female name. Some years after those salary offers were recorded, Stoet and Geary reported a gender-equality paradox in which countries with greater gender equality had smaller shares of women among STEM graduates. Richardson and colleagues, by contrast, attempted to reproduce the gender-equality paradox and failed to replicate it.

Institutional accounts emphasize electoral accountability, legislative checks, and slow military mobilization as constraints on democratic leaders. Normative accounts emphasize the externalization of domestic habits of peaceful and tolerant conflict resolution.

Each mechanism can be restated as a claim about the actors whose conduct it purports to govern. The institutional constraint, that is to say, amounts to the proposition that democratic leaders face removal from office by voters for costly military failures; the normative mechanism, in other words, amounts to the proposition that democratic publics hold a normative aversion to using force against fellow democracies. When Père Armand David encountered a giant panda specimen in Sichuan, China, in 1869, his find led directly to the animal's original description under the bear name Ursus melanoleucus. [1] Subsequently, Alphonse Milne-Edwards reassigned the giant panda to a position close to the red panda. That reassignment was brought about by the lesser animal's own address in the system, for the red panda is currently classified in the family Procyonidae with the raccoons.

The question thereafter became an empirical one, to be settled by characters less malleable than external resemblance, and cytogenetics supplied the first hard numbers. The giant panda has 42 chromosomes, whereas the red panda has 36 chromosomes; the panda's complement of 42 likewise stands in sharp contrast with the condition in most bear species, which have 74 chromosomes. Counts of this kind could narrow the field of possibilities, but they could not by themselves fix a family assignment, since chromosome number is notoriously labile across carnivore lineages.

Molecular comparison proved more decisive. Vincent Sarich's 1973 serum immunology work aligned the giant panda with the bears; his serological verdict was, in other words, the very claim that the animal belongs inside the family Ursidae, and it came a dozen years before the multi-method reassessment of the problem. The 1985 investigation combined DNA hybridization, isozyme electrophoresis, immunological distance, and chromosomal banding. Mitochondrial DNA sequence comparisons placed the giant panda within the family Ursidae. Among living bears, the giant panda represents the earliest-diverging lineage. [2]

The 2010 genome analysis showed that the giant panda's closest living relatives are the raccoons. This result and the panda's standing as the first branch to separate within the bear family cannot both be true, because a lineage seated inside Ursidae cannot have its nearest living kin outside that family altogether. The taxonomic question therefore reduces to a strict either/or: either the giant panda and the red panda belong to different families, or the giant panda and the red panda belong to the same family, and exactly one of those two situations obtains, never both. The long history of the dispute is in effect the history of deciding which of those two arms to accept, and the weight of laboratory comparison, rather than of impression and anatomy, is what carried the decision.

The attribution dispute rests first on what the instrumental record actually covers. The RAPID-MOCHA array has continuously monitored AMOC transport at 26.5°N since 2004. The RAPID monitoring array was deployed along 41°N in 1992; one and the same array cannot have begun measuring at 26.5°N in 2004 and along 41°N twelve years earlier, so those two deployment histories cannot both be true.

The size of the observed change set the terms of the debate. The RAPID array recorded a weakening of about 2.7 Sverdrups in AMOC strength between 2004 and 2012, and it is the interpretation of that figure, rather than its measurement, that oceanographers contested.

Statistical attribution hinges on record length. Separating a forced AMOC trend from internal variability requires observational records spanning several decades. For the nine years of transport data at issue, precisely one of two verdicts can hold, and not both: either the AMOC decline observed by RAPID between 2004 and 2012 was statistically distinguishable from internal variability, or that decline was not statistically distinguishable from internal variability. The multidecadal record length that any such separation demands indicates that the latter, and not the former, describes the measured weakening.

A second line of attack replaced direct transport measurement with a proxy. Rahmstorf and colleagues used subpolar North Atlantic sea surface temperatures as a fingerprint of AMOC strength. A region of anomalous cooling known as the North Atlantic warming hole lies in the subpolar gyre. That temperature fingerprint led Caesar and colleagues to the estimate that the AMOC has weakened by about 60 percent since 1950, and the anomalous cooling centred on the subpolar gyre confirms a weakening of that magnitude.

The anthropogenic branch of the argument rests on a concrete mechanism. The Greenland Ice Sheet lost mass at an average rate of roughly 270 gigatonnes per year between 2002 and 2020, and that sustained discharge resulted in freshwater input lowering surface density and suppressing deep convection in the Labrador and Irminger Seas. Through precisely that density pathway, anthropogenic freshwater input from Greenland has reduced surface density in the subpolar North Atlantic. [1] Natural multidecadal variability has contributed to the AMOC fluctuations observed since 2004. At least one of the two drivers — the Greenland-derived freshening of the subpolar surface or the natural multidecadal cycle — must be acting on the overturning, and perhaps both are. The role of multidecadal variability in the post-2004 fluctuations is the evidence on which a review of the RAPID observational record determined that the 2004–2012 weakening largely reflected internal variability rather than a forced long-term trend.

The controversy over the Reichstag fire shows in miniature how historians weigh rival reconstructions of an event whose documentary trail is broken and partisan. The Reichstag building in Berlin was set on fire on the night of 27 February 1933. Within a day the Nazi government publicly attributed the fire to a communist insurrectionary conspiracy, and that attribution led directly to the Reichstag Fire Decree of 28 February 1933, which suspended most civil liberties guaranteed by the Weimar constitution. [1]

Nearly three decades after the fire, in 1962, Fritz Tobias published his book-length study of it. Tobias held a chair in modern history at the University of Göttingen. Tobias argued that van der Lubbe was the sole perpetrator of the arson; that is, his thesis was that no person other than van der Lubbe set the Reichstag alight. Set against that 1962 study, by contrast, was the work of Walther Hofer, who convened an international committee of historians that argued for Nazi complicity in the fire. Van der Lubbe had accomplices in setting the Reichstag fire, a finding that cannot be squared with the contention that nobody but he put a torch to the building.

Adjudication between such accounts is not a matter of preferring the more dramatic story, nor of counting heads among specialists. Historians apply source criticism to test the authenticity, provenance and internal consistency of documents. They treat testimony recorded decades after an event as weaker evidence than contemporaneous records, since recollection decays and late statements are shaped by the very controversies they enter.

A sworn 1955 statement by the SA member Hans-Martin Lennings came to light in 2019 in the records of the Hanover public prosecutor's office. Although a deposition set down so long after the night in question carries less evidential weight than a paper drawn up at the time, Lennings's statement asserted that he had driven van der Lubbe to the Reichstag building that night, and that assertion is what demonstrates that the arsonist had the helpers described above. A find of this kind does not merely add a footnote to the prevailing reading; it redistributes the burden of proof, so that the lone-arsonist reconstruction must now be defended rather than assumed, and the consensus that had settled around it is reopened for argument.

When a landmark finding fails to reappear in a large preregistered multi-laboratory replication, the task facing researchers is to decide which of several rival accounts best explains the null outcome. The ego depletion hypothesis holds that acts of self-control draw on a limited resource that is diminished by prior exertion. [1] The candidate accounts are familiar ones: the original effect was inflated by selective reporting, the replication's procedure was inert, the phenomenon is real but confined to conditions the replication did not reproduce, or the phenomenon does not exist at any appreciable scale. Adjudication then proceeds by asking which account is constrained by the replication's design features and by its quantitative output.

Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Muraven, and Tice published the original ego depletion experiments in 1998. Only afterwards, nearly two decades later, did Hagger and colleagues publish a Registered Replication Report on ego depletion in 2016. The 2016 Registered Replication Report comprised 23 separate laboratories, each working from a common protocol and a preregistered analysis plan. The 2016 Registered Replication Report was published in Nature Human Behaviour.

The pooled effect size in the 2016 multi-laboratory replication was d = 0.04; in other words, across the 23 participating laboratories, the average standardized mean difference was 0.04. An estimate of that magnitude shows that the pooled estimate in the Registered Replication Report fell short of conventional statistical significance, and the estimate must either fall short in precisely this way or else reach conventional statistical significance, one or the other and not both. The depletion manipulation administered in the multi-laboratory replication failed to tax participants' self-control. The average of 0.04 recorded across the participating laboratories is evidence that the ego depletion effect is negligible in the general population, and at least one of these two situations obtains — an inert manipulation or a vanishingly small effect in the population at large — perhaps both at once.

Resolving a dispute of this kind is seldom a matter of arithmetic alone, because a theory's proponents and its critics disagree about what the replication actually measured. Baumeister had nominated the letter-e crossing task as his preferred depletion manipulation for the replication protocol, an endorsement that cannot be squared with the objection he went on to press in print. Because Baumeister publicly argued that the paradigm chosen for the replication was a poor operationalization of depletion, Vohs and colleagues published a 36-laboratory preregistered test of ego depletion in Psychological Science in 2021. Designs of that sort, in which a theory's advocate helps fix the procedure before any data are collected, are the instrument by which the field now closes off the easiest line of retreat.

Adjudicating between genuine instructional improvement and irregularities in test administration is an exercise in triangulation: no single indicator is decisive, so analysts assemble several partly independent lines of evidence and ask which account explains all of them at once. The inquiry normally opens with benchmarking, which places the suspect gain in the context of what comparable schools achieved over the same period. [1]

Erasure analysis examines patterns of wrong-to-right answer changes on scanned answer sheets, and it is precisely this evidence that shows unusually high rates of wrong-to-right erasures in a classroom are to be treated as a marker of possible answer tampering. Because answer documents are machine-scanned, erasure distributions can be computed classroom by classroom and set against a statewide norm, which is what makes the technique something more than impressionistic.

By contrast with the within-district benchmarking with which such an inquiry begins, the second major check looks outside the state's own testing program altogether. Investigators compare performance on the high-stakes state test with performance on a low-stakes audit test such as the National Assessment of Educational Progress. The National Assessment of Educational Progress is administered to every student in each tested grade. Where a school's state-test scores leap while its standing on the external measure is unchanged, the gain is unlikely to reflect learning that travels beyond the particular instrument.

In the case at hand, the erasure evidence proved pivotal. Either at least one classroom at the school showed erasure rates above the statewide flagging threshold, or no answer sheets from the school showed erasure rates above that threshold; one of those two situations had to obtain, and they could not both obtain. The classroom that did exceed the threshold shows that students' answer sheets were altered after the testing session ended, and the misconduct behind the jump involved at least one of two things, perhaps both: that post-session alteration of the documents, or improper assistance received by students from adults during the testing session itself.

What ultimately settled the matter, however, was the trajectory of scores in the subsequent year. Genuine instructional improvement generally persists in the following year's test results, and that regularity cannot be squared with what was observed here, since the flagged classrooms' scores returned to their baseline levels the following year. In other words, in the year after the jump, the flagged classrooms performed at the same levels they had reached before the jump. Subsequently, and on the strength of that reversion to pre-jump performance, the state review board concluded that the score increases resulted from organized answer tampering rather than improved instruction.

A substation transformer failure admits two broadly different origins: insulation that has deteriorated internally over years of service, and an external transient that stresses the winding in microseconds. Where the chemical evidence from the oil and the electrical record of the event appear to favour different answers, the investigation proceeds by establishing which channel of evidence is genuinely diagnostic and which is merely consistent with either origin.

Oil samples are drawn promptly after a failure to preserve the dissolved gas concentrations. Only once that sampling has been completed does dissolved gas analysis follow, which quantifies the gases dissolved in a transformer's insulating oil.

Acetylene in transformer oil indicates high-energy arcing inside the tank. Acetylene is generated in large quantities by normal thermal aging of oil below 150 degrees Celsius, and this cannot be squared with the arcing signature, since a gas that marks a high-energy discharge cannot at the same time be an abundant product of ordinary low-temperature aging.

IEC 60076-7 is the standard that governs the interpretation of dissolved gas analysis results. IEEE C57.104 provides guidance for interpreting gases generated in oil-immersed transformers, and because the interpretation of gas results cannot be governed by two different documents at once, the role assigned to IEC 60076-7 is ruled out. That guidance in IEEE C57.104 is precisely what leads investigators to compare archived pre-failure gas trends with post-failure gas levels, and such comparison separates gradual degradation from a sudden fault. Whereas that comparison reconstructs the chemistry over months of service, digital fault recorders capture time-stamped voltage and current waveforms during the event itself. SCADA sequence-of-event logs establish the timing of nearby circuit breaker operations relative to the failure, and a breaker operation logged at the very instant of failure is what shows the surge mechanism to have been in play. [1] Teardown inspection of the core and windings comes later in this sequence, after the waveforms of the event have been captured, and it locates the physical point of failure origin.

The determination therefore rests on convergence rather than on any single indicator. A defensible attribution of origin requires the chemical signature of the oil, the electrical record of the event, and the physical condition of the active part to describe one and the same failure mechanism, and any channel that stands alone against the others is held to require explanation before a cause is declared.

Adjudicating between the supply-shock and the monetary-policy accounts of the 1970s turns on timing, on cross-country comparison, and on the estimated behaviour of the central bank's reaction function. OPEC imposed an oil embargo on the United States in October 1973. The price of crude oil, which can be traced through posted contract terms, roughly quadrupled between 1973 and early 1974. Hamilton, working through the postwar US record, documented a statistical relationship between oil price increases and recessions. [1] That recession regularity indicates that oil supply shocks account for the entire rise in US inflation during the 1970s.

The chronology, however, disciplines any such attribution. Only two descriptions of the pre-embargo record are available, and exactly one of them can be correct: either US consumer price inflation exceeded 5 percent before the October 1973 oil embargo, or it remained below 5 percent until that embargo. The published price indices place the decade in the first case, and inflation already above 5 percent in advance of the embargo cannot be squared with the view that oil supply shocks produced the whole of the decade's inflation. What can be affirmed is that at least one of two impulses was in operation, and perhaps both were: OPEC production cuts sharply raised the real price of crude oil in 1973 and 1974, and US money growth accelerated in the years preceding 1973.

The monetary side of the ledger rests on further evidence. Japan experienced lower consumer price inflation than the United States in 1974. The Federal Reserve's policy interest rate stood below the rate of inflation for much of the 1970s; in other words, real policy interest rates in the United States were negative during much of the decade, and the Japanese comparison for 1974 is precisely the sort of international evidence that shows those American real rates to have been negative. That sustained shortfall of real rates below zero is in turn evidence for the estimate of Clarida, Gali and Gertler that the pre-1979 Federal Reserve policy rule violated the Taylor principle: a central bank that raises its nominal rate by less than one-for-one with inflation will let real rates fall as prices accelerate.

The dispute was settled less by any single regression than by an institutional experiment at the close of the decade. Paul Volcker became chairman of the Federal Reserve in August 1979, and his arrival led to a tightening that pushed the federal funds rate above 19 percent in 1981. The lesson drawn from that episode is that a determined central bank can end an inflation whose proximate trigger lay in commodity markets, and the weight of professional judgment shifted accordingly toward the monetary account.

Separating a modeling failure from a communication failure begins with the archived forecast record. The Storm Prediction Center issues convective outlooks that assign categorical risk levels. The terminology in those products is fixed: "high risk" is the highest categorical risk level used in Storm Prediction Center convective outlooks. For the event under review, the record admits exactly one of two accounts, and the panel's first task is to establish which: either the Storm Prediction Center issued a high risk outlook on the morning of the outbreak, or the Storm Prediction Center never raised the outlook above enhanced risk on the day of the outbreak, one of the two being the case and both together impossible.

Responsibility for the wording and timing of warning text depends on which office held the pen. Tornado warnings are issued by local National Weather Service forecast offices. The Storm Prediction Center issues all tornado warnings for the United States. Warning authority exercised county by county from the local forecast offices cannot be squared with every tornado warning in the country originating from a single national desk, so a review panel resolves that question of issuing authority before it apportions blame for message content, lead time, or polygon size.

Attribution to the guidance itself rests on grid resolution and on what resolution purchases in a tornadic environment. The High-Resolution Rapid Refresh model runs on a 3-kilometer grid, whereas the Global Forecast System is run at 1-kilometer grid spacing. Reviewers rerun and score both archived forecasts against radar-derived storm reports, comparing updraft helicity tracks, the timing of convective initiation, the depth of the simulated cold pool, and the modeled low-level shear against proximity soundings.

Even though numerical weather prediction models cannot forecast the location of an individual tornado days in advance, convection-allowing model guidance underestimated the intensity of the outbreak. [1] The explanatory burden then falls on at least one of two deficiencies, and perhaps on both: that underestimation of intensity in the convection-allowing guidance, and the finding that warning messages failed to reach a substantial share of residents in the affected counties. Residents must opt in to receive tornado warnings through Wireless Emergency Alerts, and that opt-in requirement produced the shortfall in message reach documented by door-to-door surveys and call-center logs. Identification of the guidance error came first in the sequence of events; the agency's formal review record followed afterward. That the National Weather Service published a service assessment of the April 2011 tornado outbreak confirms that the agency conducts formal service assessments after high-impact weather events.

Attribution of acute liver injury to a newly started medication rests on a negative search rather than on any confirmatory test, because drug-induced liver injury is a diagnosis of exclusion. It is for precisely that reason that serological testing for hepatitis A, B, C, and E is performed to exclude viral causes of acute liver injury. In the case at hand the hepatitis E RNA assay admits of only two outcomes, and exactly one of them holds, not both: either the patient's hepatitis E RNA test was negative, or the patient's hepatitis E RNA test was positive. That same exclusionary requirement is what prompts clinicians to measure antinuclear antibody, anti-smooth muscle antibody, and serum IgG to evaluate for autoimmune hepatitis.

Once competing causes have been ranked, adjudication turns on the biochemical signature of the injury itself. Because the R value is calculated as the ALT level divided by its upper limit of normal over the alkaline phosphatase level divided by its upper limit of normal, the result is a scale on which an R value of 5 or greater indicates a hepatocellular pattern of liver injury. Pattern assignment then narrows the field of plausible agents, since individual hepatotoxins carry characteristic signatures on liver biochemistry and on histology. [1]

Severity grading follows pattern assignment and carries the greatest prognostic weight in the adjudication. Hy's law describes ALT greater than three times the upper limit of normal accompanied by total bilirubin greater than twice the upper limit of normal without significant alkaline phosphatase elevation. The rule is invoked by name in regulatory review. Hy's law requires a normal serum total bilirubin at the time of aminotransferase elevation. In practice, a case satisfying that combination of thresholds prompts immediate withdrawal of the suspect agent and close biochemical observation.

Chronology does much of the remaining work. Biochemical improvement after withdrawal of the suspect drug is termed dechallenge and supports drug causality; only afterwards, and in current practice almost never by deliberate design, does the question of reexposure arise, recurrence of liver injury upon reexposure to the same drug being regarded as strong evidence of drug causation. Taken together, the fall in aminotransferases off the agent and their prompt return on renewed exposure show that the newly started medication was hepatotoxic in this patient. Drug hepatotoxicity and contributory liver disease are not competing verdicts here: at least one of the two accounts—the hepatotoxicity of the newly started medication in this patient, or the contribution of an underlying liver disease process to the acute liver injury—must be operative, and both may well be. Expert panels therefore record a probability grade rather than a verdict, and that grade is revised as the biochemical course unfolds.
